chapterNote: The book opens in the glittering, wine-soaked court of Persia, where the king's word is law and a queen is deposed for saying no. God is never named in Esther — not once in ten chapters — yet the empty throne left by Vashti's fall is the first quiet turn of a providence that will place a Jewish girl exactly where she is needed. Every human calculation here is about honor and control; the unseen Hand is already at work beneath it.

1.text: It happened in the days of Ahasuerus — the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Cush over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces —
1.notes: Ahasuerus (Hebrew 'Achashverosh, H325) is the Persian Xerxes I. India to Cush (Ethiopia/upper Nile) marks the full breadth of the empire; a hundred and twenty-seven provinces underscores a reach so vast that a single decree can touch every corner — which will matter terribly, and then wonderfully, before the book is done.

2.text: In those days, when King Ahasuerus was seated on his royal throne in the fortress of Susa,

3.text: in the third year of his reign he gave a banquet for all his officials and courtiers. The commanders of Persia and Media, the nobles, and the governors of the provinces were gathered before him,
3.notes: birah (H1002) = fortified acropolis; Susa (Shushan) was the empire's winter capital. The third year (c. 483 BC) sets the feast just before Xerxes' famous campaign against Greece — this is a king marshaling and dazzling his whole realm.

4.text: and for many days — a hundred and eighty in all — he put on show the glorious wealth of his kingdom and the dazzling splendor of his greatness.
4.amp: he displayed the wealth of his glorious kingdom [kavod (H3519) — weighty glory, honor] and the splendor [yeqar (H3366) — costly magnificence] of his greatness, day after day, a hundred and eighty days.

5.text: When those days were over, the king held a banquet lasting seven days for all the people who were in the fortress of Susa, from the greatest to the least, in the courtyard of the garden of the royal palace.

6.text: Hangings of white and violet linen were fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings on marble columns; couches of gold and silver stood on a mosaic pavement of porphyry and marble, of mother-of-pearl and colored stone.
6.notes: The verse lingers on the opulence deliberately — Persia's power is measured here in fabric and stone. It is a world of surfaces and display, and into it the story will smuggle a hidden faithfulness that owns none of this.

7.text: Drinks were served in golden goblets, no two of them alike, and royal wine flowed without limit, as befitted a king's bounty.

8.text: By the king's order the drinking followed no compulsion, for he had charged every steward of his house to let each man do just as he pleased.
8.notes: A court ruled entirely by the king's will — even its freedoms are decreed. The same absolute royal word that here indulges every guest will soon be turned, by Haman's hand, into an edict of death.

9.text: Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the royal house that belonged to King Ahasuerus.

10.text: On the seventh day, when the king's heart was merry with wine, he ordered Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carkas — the seven eunuchs who waited in the presence of King Ahasuerus —

11.text: to bring Queen Vashti before the king wearing the royal crown, to show the peoples and the officials her beauty; for she was lovely to look upon.

12.text: But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command brought by the eunuchs. The king was enraged, and his fury burned within him.
12.notes: The text never says why Vashti refused — to be paraded before drunken men was demeaning, but Scripture leaves her reasons silent. What matters for the story is the hinge: her 'no' empties a throne, and an empty throne is exactly what Providence will use.

13.text: So the king turned to the wise men who understood the times — for it was his custom to lay a matter before all who were versed in law and judgment —

14.text: and closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media who had access to the king and held the first rank in the kingdom.
14.notes: "Who saw the king's face" (rendered here 'had access to the king') was a Persian idiom for the innermost circle of counselors — the seven with the right to enter the royal presence unbidden. Their advice will reshape the empire's law over a single dinner-party quarrel.

15.text: "By law, what should be done with Queen Vashti," he asked, "for failing to obey the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"

16.text: Then Memucan spoke up before the king and the princes: "Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but every official and every people in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.
16.notes: Memucan inflates a private slight into an empire-wide emergency — the courtier's instinct to magnify. The whole apparatus of Persian law is about to be mobilized over wounded male pride, a comedy of overreaction that the narrator lets speak for itself.

17.text: For the queen's conduct will get out to all the women, and they will look with contempt on their own husbands, saying, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she would not come.'

18.text: This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's conduct will say the same to all the king's officials — and there will be no end of contempt and quarreling.

19.text: If it please the king, let a royal edict go out from him, written into the laws of Persia and Media so that it cannot be revoked, that Vashti shall never again come before King Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal place to another woman better than she.
19.amp: let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes so that it cannot pass away [lo' ya'avor (H5674) — it shall not be crossed or repealed]; the irrevocable law of the Medes and Persians.
19.notes: Here is the empire's fateful peculiarity: a law once sealed 'cannot be revoked' (dath, H1881, the Medo-Persian statute). That very rigidity will nearly doom the Jews when Haman's decree is sealed (3:12–13), and then become their rescue when the counter-decree is sealed with equal permanence (8:8).

20.text: When the king's decree is proclaimed throughout his vast realm, then all the wives will give honor to their husbands, from the greatest to the least."

21.text: The advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did just as Memucan had said.

22.text: He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, that every man should be master in his own house and speak according to the language of his own people.
22.notes: The empire's flawless postal machinery — letters to every province in every script — is introduced here on a trivial errand. The same swift couriers will later carry both a death-warrant and its undoing across the same roads. Even the mechanics of the court are being quietly set in place.
